title: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 Review: Radeon 8065S Outshines 8060S in Gaming Performance
body:
The latest benchmark results for AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 platform have revealed a noticeable performance edge for the Radeon 8065S over its sibling, the 8060S, marking a significant step forward for the company’s integrated‑graphics strategy. In a series of Gorgon Halo gaming tests, the 8065S delivered 104 frames per second in Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p on High settings, while synthetic scores in 3DMark Time Spy were up to 11.8 percent higher than those recorded by the 8060S configuration. The data underscores AMD’s push to make high‑end integrated GPUs a viable alternative for gamers and creators who demand strong performance without the cost and power draw of a discrete graphics card.

The Gorgon Halo processor, which powers the Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, is built on AMD’s latest Zen 5 architecture and integrates a next‑generation RDNA 3‑based GPU. What sets the new chip apart is its support for an unprecedented 192 GB of unified memory, with up to 160 GB of that pool directly addressable by the integrated graphics engine. This massive memory ceiling, while far beyond typical consumer needs, gives the GPU a substantial buffer for high‑resolution textures, large AI models, and future‑proofing for workloads that rely heavily on shared memory bandwidth. In practical terms, the extra memory translates into smoother frame rates in texture‑intensive titles and more headroom for AI‑enhanced features such as AMD’s Ryzen AI acceleration.

The Cyberpunk 2077 test is particularly telling because the game is known for its demanding ray‑tracing and DLSS‑style upscaling requirements. Achieving 104 fps at 1080p High without any external GPU demonstrates that the 8065S can handle modern, graphically intensive titles at playable rates, a realm previously reserved for low‑to‑mid‑range discrete cards. Moreover, the 11.8 percent uplift in 3DMark Time Spy—AMD’s own benchmark that stresses both compute and graphics pipelines—suggests that the performance gain is not limited to a single game but is indicative of broader improvements in rasterization, compute shaders, and memory handling.

Analysts see this development as a strategic move to capture a growing segment of the market that values compact, power‑efficient devices without sacrificing visual fidelity. Laptops, mini‑PCs, and even all‑in‑one desktops can now be equipped with a single‑chip solution that rivals entry‑level dedicated GPUs. For OEMs, the ability to offer a system with 192 GB of unified memory simplifies board design, reduces component count, and potentially lowers BOM costs. For end users, the benefit is a lighter, quieter machine that can still run the latest games, stream high‑resolution video, and perform AI‑driven tasks such as real‑time translation or image enhancement.

However, the performance gap between the 8065S and the 8060S also highlights the importance of SKU differentiation within AMD’s integrated‑graphics lineup. While the 8065S’s advantage is clear, the 8060S still lags behind many entry‑level discrete cards, and its real‑world impact will depend on pricing and availability. Competitors such as Intel’s Xe‑HPG integrated solutions are also advancing rapidly, meaning AMD must maintain a compelling value proposition to stay ahead. Additionally, the massive unified memory pool could raise questions about system configuration and cost, as most consumer platforms will not need—or be able to afford—such large allocations.

Looking ahead, the Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 and its Radeon 8065S GPU set a new benchmark for what integrated graphics can achieve. As software developers increasingly incorporate AI‑assisted rendering and as game engines become more efficient at leveraging shared memory, the line between integrated and discrete performance will continue to blur. If AMD can keep scaling memory bandwidth and AI acceleration while keeping power consumption in check, the 8065S could become the cornerstone of a new generation of thin‑and‑light gaming laptops and compact workstations, reshaping expectations for performance‑centric, all‑in‑one computing solutions.
